name: TiDB
summary: A distributed SQL system with stateless MySQL-compatible compute nodes, a Placement Driver for cluster metadata and timestamps, and TiKV-backed transactional storage with coprocessor pushdown.

features.name: Stateless distributed SQL compute
features.description: TiDB Server exposes the MySQL protocol, parses and optimizes SQL, builds distributed plans, sends key-value work to storage, and assembles results without storing table data locally.
benefits: Compute nodes scale horizontally behind a load balancer
Separates SQL planning and execution from persistent storage
costs: Distributed plans and RPCs add network coordination
Compute capacity and storage capacity must be scaled and tuned separately

features.name: Placement Driver coordinated storage
features.description: The Placement Driver stores cluster and TiKV distribution metadata, allocates transaction timestamps, and schedules data according to the reported state of storage nodes.
benefits: Centralizes placement knowledge and scheduling decisions
Provides a timestamp oracle for MVCC transaction ordering
costs: PD availability and metadata freshness constrain cluster coordination
Scheduling and timestamp services add a control-plane dependency

features.name: Ordered key-value mapping with coprocessors
features.description: TiDB maps table rows and indexes to ordered TiKV key ranges and can push predicates and partial aggregations toward storage nodes to reduce result transfer.
benefits: Preserves range-scan access to relational rows and indexes
Reduces network transfer for selective and aggregate distributed queries
costs: Key encoding couples relational access paths to the storage keyspace
Pushdown support and plan shape affect performance and semantics

mathematical_views.question: How does a table and its indexes refine into ordered key ranges while preserving point lookup and scan semantics?
assumptions: Table, row, and index identifiers are stable within the modeled schema version
Key encoding preserves the intended ordering for range scans
The view abstracts TiKV replication and RocksDB layout

mathematical_views.question: How do PD timestamps, TiKV transactions, and SQL-layer commit modes constrain the observable order of distributed changes?
assumptions: TSO physical and logical components are monotonic for the modeled allocation path
Transaction isolation and commit mode are explicit inputs
The view does not infer stronger guarantees than the selected mode documents

benefits: Independent horizontal scaling of SQL compute
costs: Network plans and remote storage calls add latency and failure modes

benefits: Explicit placement, scheduling, and timestamp control plane
costs: Control-plane health and coordination are prerequisites for some operations

benefits: Efficient ordered access and reduced distributed query transfer
costs: Storage key layout and pushdown capability constrain execution choices
